content: Rex1, also known as Zfp-42, is a well-established marker of pluripotency and is predominantly expressed in undifferentiated embryonic stem cells. Beyond serving as a marker, its regulation is essential for maintaining the pluripotent state. As cells begin to differentiate, Rex1 expression is rapidly and significantly downregulated. Discovery Rex1 was first identified in 1989 by Hosler, BA, et al., during their studies on F9 murine teratocarcinoma stem cells. These cells were found to express high levels of Rex1 and exhibited characteristics similar to pluripotent stem cells of the inner cell mass (ICM). When exposed to retinoic acid (RA), these teratocarcinoma stem cells differentiated into non-tumorigenic cells resembling the extraembryonic endoderm of early mouse embryos. The nucleotide sequence of Rex1 was isolated using differential hybridization of an F9 cell. The name Rex1 (Reduced Expression 1) was chosen because its mRNA levels declined significantly within 12 hours of RA addition. Structure Rex1 is a protein encoded by the ZFP42 gene in humans. It consists of 310 amino acids and contains four closely spaced zinc finger domains located at positions 188–212, 217–239, 245–269, and 275–299. p38 MAPK and Mesenchymal Stem Cells Rex1 plays a critical role in maintaining the proliferative state of mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) while simultaneously preventing their differentiation. High levels of Rex1 are expressed in umbilical cord blood MSCs and adipose MSCs, whereas bone marrow MSCs exhibit low Rex1 expression. The rate of proliferation in MSCs is strongly correlated with Rex1 expression levels, with higher Rex1 expression associated with increased proliferation. MSCs with low Rex1 expression show activation of p38 MAPK and elevated levels of MKK3. Thus, Rex1 expression is inversely correlated with p38 MAPK activation and positively correlated with high proliferation rates. Rex1 inhibits MKK3 expression, which activates p38 MAPK. Activated p38 MAPK, in turn, suppresses proliferation. Additionally, Rex1 inhibits the transcription factors NOTCH and STAT3, both of which promote differentiation. Therefore, Rex1 supports high proliferation rates and prevents differentiation through a regulatory network involving various transcription factors and protein kinases. Embryo Development Tissue Derivation During embryogenesis, the inner cell mass (ICM) separates from the trophectoderm. Stem cells derived from the ICM and trophectoderm express high levels of Oct3/4 and Rex1. As the ICM matures into the epiblast and primitive ectoderm, the cells within the ICM become a heterogeneous population with varying levels of Rex1 expression. Cells lacking both Rex1 and Oct3/4 (Rex1−/Oct3/4−) differentiate into trophectoderm, while cells expressing both Rex1 and Oct3/4 (Rex1+/Oct3/4+) predominantly differentiate into primitive endoderm and mesoderm. Cells that are Rex1−/Oct3/4+ differentiate into primitive ectoderm, which gives rise to somatic cell lineages. Gene Control Studies have shown that Rex1 regulates downstream targets such as PEG3 and Nespas. Rex1 controls the expression of Peg3 through epigenetic modifications. YY1 has been implicated in establishing DNA methylation on the maternal allele of PEG3 during oogenesis. Rex1 protects the paternal allele from methylation, ensuring that the PEG3 gene remains unmethylated during early embryogenesis. Through its epigenetic regulation of genes like PEG3, Rex1 plays a critical role in embryonic development and fetal growth rates. Expression in Adult Tissues Rex1 expression in adult tissues has been identified exclusively in the testes. In situ hybridization studies have shown that spermatocytes in the inner layers of the testes express Rex1. These male germ cells undergoing meiosis are the specific cells in the testes that express Rex1. However, Rex1 expression has not been observed in female germ cells. Rex1 Interactions with Other Transcription Factors Rex1 is part of a transcription factor network that regulates itself and other factors through varying expression levels. Nanog Nanog acts as a transcriptional activator of the Rex1 promoter and is crucial for sustaining Rex1 expression. Knockdown of Nanog in embryonic stem cells reduces Rex1 expression, while forced expression of Nanog stimulates Rex1 expression. Nanog regulates Rex1 transcription through two strong transactivation domains on its C-terminus, which are necessary for activating the Rex1 promoter. NOTCH Rex1 inhibits the expression of NOTCH, thereby preventing differentiation. STAT3 Rex1 also inhibits the expression of STAT3, further preventing differentiation. Sox2 Rex1 is cooperatively regulated by Sox2 and Nanog. Oct3/4 Oct3/4 exhibits dual regulatory effects on the Rex1 promoter. In cells with high Oct3/4 expression, exogenous Oct3/4 represses Rex1. Conversely, in cells with low or no Oct3/4 expression, exogenous Oct3/4 activates Rex1. This dual regulatory ability implies that at low Oct3/4 protein levels, the Rex1 promoter is activated, while at high Oct3/4 protein levels, the Rex1 promoter is repressed.
